# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

Platform: iPadOS. Video autoplays loudly, overlays cover captions, scrubbing discards the transcript position and a network stall looks like a paused video. People may switch to picture-in-picture where supported.

# Apple HIG: End-to-end behavior and recovery

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Trace the person’s task from entry through completion, cancellation, interruption and recovery. Select the pattern procedure for the actual failure or desired behavior before selecting its controls.
2. Preserve the current work, selection and navigation context across the transitions that matter. Choose interruption or modality according to urgency and task scope, not visual emphasis.
3. For asynchronous or recurring work, separate current progress, eventual result, error recovery and unavailable capability. For audio/video/haptics, specify user control and environmental behavior.
4. Deliver a transition/state specification, a correction to the supplied flow, or ranked findings tied to observed steps. Test alternate exits and resumption, not just the success path.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

name: apple-hig-playing-video
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting video playback controls, aspect behavior, TV-app handoff, exit context, and spatial or watch presentation.

# Preserve playback intent across entry and exit

Read [the video guide](../../references/playing-video.md). This workflow is application advice; the source's overlapping 2:1 aspect endpoint must not become an invented exclusive rule.

Inspect content aspect/duration, controls, resume state, entry/exit destinations, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Identify system-player use versus a justified custom need. Record real transport/keyboard/remote behavior; a poster or mock control does not prove playback support.

Prefer system players and preserve original aspect without baked-in bars. Use system aspect behavior at the source's ambiguous boundary. Keep useful metadata unobtrusive and extra actions close to playback. Honor Space/remote conventions and secondary-audio hints. For TV-app entry begin/resume the requested content directly with its supplied profile, preparing an in-app exit destination immediately so even a quick exit is coherent. Avoid unnecessary splash/detail barriers and show honest loading only when needed. On TV keep overlays restrained and use the documented delay before an interactive overlay pauses playback. On visionOS start by choice in a modest resizable window, never force immersion, and preserve system control space; inline video remains 2D. Watch clips should be short with suitable unscaled assets rather than a phone player compressed onto the wrist.

Implement playback/entry/exit states or supply transport/aspect/resume specifications; reviews identify exact control, crop, or context failures. Keep encoding/dimension tables in the reference.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a TV-app launch opens a branded detail screen, restarts a long film, and exits to nowhere when Back is pressed quickly. Decision: the playback request already carries intent. After: resume directly at the retained position/profile and prepare the corresponding in-app detail/menu before playback begins.

Deliver the artifact and entry, resume, controls, aspect, loading, and exit contract. Verify quick exit, PiP, different aspect ratios, interruption, overlays, and supported input. Fail for lost resume position, baked-in cropping/bars, forced immersion, or a missing exit context. Native media, audio routing, captions, and comfort need runtime/device evidence.

name: apple-hig-playing-audio
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting audio sessions, output routes, silence, interruptions, media controls, and spatial sound behavior.

# Respect the output and interruption the person chose

Read [the audio guide](../../references/playing-audio.md), including the audio-category table. This workflow is application advice; do not infer playback or microphone behavior from UI alone.

Inspect essential/incidental audio purpose, playback/recording state, route/category configuration, interruptions, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Distinguish deliberate media from incidental feedback and sustained competing playback from resumable interruption.

Choose the category matching silence/mixing/background needs rather than globally raising volume. Respect output selection; reroute smoothly on connection and pause on headphone disconnection for privacy. Expose supported output/volume controls and respond to external playback commands only in a relevant context without stealing another app's controls. Specify interruption resume based on actual system signals/user intent; a new playlist is not a brief ducking event. Recording/call policy needs explicit handling, including not automatically unmuting a VoIP session after a closed-folio microphone interruption. On TV do not add automatic notification sounds. In visionOS complement essential spatial cues visually, preserve native control sounds, and distinguish Now Playing window closure from attention ducking. Watch short/long playback and system Now Playing have their own supported behavior.

Implement the session/route/interruption contract, produce it as a state specification, or review exact privacy/coexistence defects. Keep category facts in the reference, not duplicated tables.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a meditation app sets global volume, resumes over a newly chosen music playlist, and plays through speakers after headphones disconnect. Decision: it overrides three user choices. After: adjust only relative mix, pause for route loss, and resume only for appropriate signaled interruptions rather than unrelated playback.

Deliver the artifact and category, route, external-control, interruption/resume contract. Verify silent mode, competing audio, headphone disconnect, temporary interruption, and recording/privacy states. Fail for unintended speaker playback, global volume changes, or unauthorized automatic resume. Actual audio routing, microphones, sound comfort, and hardware behavior need device tests.

name: apple-hig-loading
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting useful partial content, placeholders, background asset loading, and unavoidable waits.
---

# Keep useful content ahead of the wait

Read [the loading guide](../../references/loading.md). This workflow is application advice; timing and download availability require implementation evidence.

Inspect content dependencies, cached/partial data, asset sizes, initial interaction, platform, and create/review/adapt mode. Separate indispensable work from independent/background work and record measured waits when available. Do not infer duration or success from a skeleton screen.

Show useful structure promptly and replace placeholders as real content arrives. Keep other features usable while loading, retaining known content where appropriate. Schedule large assets nondisruptively with supported background mechanisms instead of blocking every startup. For unavoidable waits beyond a moment, communicate ongoing work and estimate only when measurable. Match optional engaging content to duration without a repetitive loop that disguises a stall. Games can use thematic loading, but truthful status/recovery still matters. On watch immediate content is preferable; brief indicators beat blank screens, while longer waits should not encourage wrist watching.

Implement content/dependency/loading states or provide a partial-content/placeholder/progress specification; reviews identify exact unnecessary blocking and misleading-placeholder defects. Define error/retry/available-data behavior according to the task rather than leaving a permanent fake skeleton.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a catalog blocks browsing until all preview videos download and replaces cached products with blank placeholders on refresh. Decision: independent assets should not remove useful content. After: show cached/current product information promptly, load previews in background, and give honest localized wait/retry feedback only for content that actually needs it.

Deliver the artifact, readiness/partial-content policy, asset schedule, and wait resolution. Verify slow/offline, partial success, refresh with existing data, retry, and completion. Fail for unnecessary whole-screen blocking, placeholders mistaken for real values, or an unresolved wait with no recovery. Report measured runtime timing separately from a proposed loading design.

Use [launching](../apple-hig-launching/SKILL.md) for startup or [progress-indicators](../../../apple-hig-status/.topics/apple-hig-progress-indicators/SKILL.md) for measurement and cancellation details.

name: apple-hig-multitasking
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting task continuity, background work, window focus, media interruptions, and simultaneous app use.

# Treat focus changes as continuity decisions

Read [the multitasking guide](../../references/multitasking.md). This workflow is application advice; do not collapse its visionOS media exception into a universal pause rule.

Inspect attention-dependent work, input-free background tasks, audio/video, saved state, target platform, and create/review/adapt request. Distinguish losing app activity, window focus, closing a window, and receiving an audio interruption. Record actual lifecycle handlers and completion sources.

Preserve context and finish eligible user-initiated input-free tasks before suspension. Notify only for important completion requiring another timely step; routine results can appear on return. Pause attention-dependent gameplay/media when appropriate, distinguishing sustained competing audio from brief directions and restoring only as justified. On iPad adapt to size without assuming access to the user's multitasking configuration. On Mac retain system key/main/layering cues. In visionOS looking at another window should not stop video merely because attention shifts; closing a Now Playing window pauses it, while closing a window backgrounds rather than quits the app. Shared Space and Full Space differ. The source does not define this mode on watchOS.

Implement lifecycle/resumption behavior or provide event-to-preservation/media/background-task contracts; reviews identify the exact event that loses work or wrongly stops/continues activity.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a spatial lecture pauses whenever someone looks at notes, while an unsent annotation disappears after closing its window. Decision: attention shift is not departure from video, and window closure is not app termination. After: let video continue on the documented focus change, preserve annotation state, and treat explicit Now Playing closure separately.

Deliver the artifact and lifecycle/event matrix with retained state and completion routes. Verify app switch, resize, competing audio, window close/reopen, and return. Fail for lost work, indiscriminate media pause/resume, or routine background completion spam. Native PiP/audio/lifecycle behavior and real background execution need runtime evidence.

Load [windows](../../../apple-hig-presentation/.topics/apple-hig-windows/SKILL.md), [playing-audio](../apple-hig-playing-audio/SKILL.md), or [playing-video](../apple-hig-playing-video/SKILL.md) for detailed handling.

# Playing video Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-video) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Prefer system players for familiar playback, aspect modes, PiP, and accessible controls. Native players exist in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, and visionOS, with TV-app integration for supported content. The source defines aspect-fill as the default for wide 2:1–2.40:1 video, potentially cropping edges, and aspect-fit for 4:3, 16:9, up to 2:1, and beyond 2.40:1, preserving the full image with bars as needed. Its exact 2:1 endpoint overlaps both statements; use system player behavior instead of inferring an exclusive boundary. TV and visionOS add transport actions and informational content tabs; spatial transport controls appear in an ornament. ## Best practices Use standard player behavior even when a genuine need requires customization. Preserve the original aspect ratio without baking in letterboxing/pillarboxing, which breaks scaling and PiP. Add only useful metadata that does not obscure playback. Honor ordinary controls, including Space to play/pause with a keyboard and expected remote gestures. Keep extra actions to a step or two; use transport controls for playback-related actions and tabs for supplemental information/recommendations. Handle secondary-audio hints so switching video/PiP and another app does not create unwanted audio mixing. ## Integrating with the TV app Match the TV app's black transition and begin/resume content directly, avoiding splash/detail screens or intro barriers. Rare required interstitials should allow Select to advance and Play to skip to content. Resume long videos at their prior stop time without asking. Honor a supplied viewer profile automatically; if absent, ask once to establish it for later. Keep Space play/pause available. ### Loading content Avoid a loading screen for quick starts. Beyond about 2 seconds, a black screen with a centered spinner and minimal other content can communicate waiting. Begin once sufficient content is ready and stream the rest in the background; any branding should remain minimal against black. ### Exiting playback Playback exits into the app, not back to TV. Show related details with resume, or a containing menu/main menu when details are unavailable. Prepare this exit context immediately after receiving the playback request so even a rapid exit is coherent. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, or macOS rules are specified. ### tvOS Keep noninteractive overlays small and brief; translucent SDR graphics reduce distraction and image-retention risk compared with bright opaque graphics. For interactive overlays, use a minimum 0.5-second delay before pausing media and presenting the overlay, and clearly offer dismissal/resumption afterward. ### visionOS Let the person start playback, begin in a modest resizable window, and keep surroundings visible for comfort. Do not automatically launch fully immersive video. In immersion, preserve the system's predictable player placement and keep virtual objects away from its controls. For scrub previews, provide 160-pixel-wide thumbnails. Inline video is 2D and should leave window content around it rather than filling the window and implying an immersive player; its controls share the plane. RealityKit video suits splash/transitional effects that need no standard playback integration and supports correct 2D/3D aspect and captions. ### watchOS System playback supports short foreground clips, inline or in a separate interface. Prefer clips no longer than 30 seconds to limit storage and wrist fatigue. Avoid scaling assets. Recommended encoding is H.264 High Profile, 160 kbps up to 30 fps; 208×260 px fullscreen portrait or 320×180 px 16:9 landscape; audio 64 kbps HE-AAC. A poster should represent actual content and invite playback without imitating an unrelated system control. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Playing audio](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio) [Feedback](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback) #### Developer documentation — AVFoundation [HTTP Live Streaming](https://developer.apple.com/streaming/) #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: September 12, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Playing audio Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Respect the person's selected output, volume, and silence state. Silent mode suppresses incidental feedback/game soundtracks but permits deliberately initiated media, alarms, and messages. System volume governs output, with separate iPhone ringer settings. Connecting headphones should reroute smoothly; disconnecting them should pause playback for privacy. ## Best practices Adjust relative mix levels without changing global volume. Permit output rerouting and use the system volume view with its output chooser. Select an audio-session category that fits the importance of sound and coexistence with other audio: | Category | Silent switch | Mixing | Background | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Solo ambient | Respected | No | No | | Ambient | Respected | Yes | No | | Playback | Ignored for essential audio | Configurable | Playback supported | | Record | Ignored | No | Recording supported | | Play and record | Ignored | Configurable | Both supported | Solo ambient suits nonessential exclusive sound; ambient lets external music coexist; playback suits media/learning; recording apps may switch to playback to review; play-and-record suits calls or messaging. Respond to external playback controls only while playing or in an appropriate audio/output context, without stealing another app's audio. Never repurpose unsupported controls. Custom players should solve needs beyond standard commands, such as unusual skip intervals or related content. When a temporary interruption ends, deactivate with notification so other apps can resume. ## Handling interruptions Choose interruption policy deliberately for recording/calls. For recording or other audio work that should continue, the app can ask the system to leave current audio uninterrupted by an incoming call unless the person accepts that call. For example, a closed iPad Smart Folio mutes the microphone and interrupts a VoIP session; end the call rather than automatically unmuting on reopen. Distinguish resumable interruptions such as calls from nonresumable choices such as a newly started playlist. A media player should resume automatically only when appropriate and signaled; a game's incidental sound can follow its gameplay resumption without the same explicit-playback check. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS Use system sound services for short sounds and vibrations. ### macOS Notification audio mixes with other sound by default. ### tvOS Audio is initiated by interaction or device calibration, rather than automatic sounds for alerts or notifications. ### visionOS Use meaningful sound to help navigation and spatial understanding, while always providing an alternative for essential information. Native controls already provide sounds; custom objects need appropriate feedback too. Spatial Audio can combine environmental ambience and localized moving or stationary sources, following a moved window. Avoid repetitive fatigue with subtle pitch/level variation, which can be randomized from one asset. Tracked sound normally reinforces an object's changing position/distance; wearer-fixed sound can suit an enveloping experience. Now Playing audio pauses when its window closes; other audio may duck when attention moves to another app. ### watchOS System-managed short clips can play in the foreground; longer audio can continue after wrist lowering or app switching. Encode audio as 64 kbps HE-AAC for quality at low data size. # Use the iPad canvas without assuming exclusive space

Read [Designing for iPadOS](../../references/designing-for-ipados.md). Inspect the task, related content, current navigation, window assumptions, and supported touch/Pencil/keyboard/pointer paths. Identify whether people hold the iPad or work at a stand/table. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode and revise only the authorized surface using the existing stack.

Decide which relationships benefit from simultaneous visibility. Keep a list beside detail or tools beside a canvas when that reduces navigation; leave unrelated information out. Replace repeated full-screen transitions or modal panels with persistent contextual structure when space permits. At compact multitasking widths, collapse that structure while retaining selection, draft, and the route back to context.

Map each meaningful operation to the inputs the task supports. Touch remains usable without attached accessories. Precise pointer selection and keyboard commands can accelerate work; Pencil may create or annotate content without becoming a required substitute for ordinary controls. Let input methods change during the same task without discarding state or hiding essential commands behind hover.

For cross-app work, specify what can be dragged out/in and where imported content lands. Treat resizing, orientation, larger text, and another app's presence as normal operating conditions. If the iPad experience runs on Mac, identify the Mac adaptation work rather than claiming identical behavior is already native.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a sheet-music editor copies its phone flow: choose score, open full-screen tools, then return to the page after each change. Decision: editing needs score and tools together, but multitasking may narrow the window. After, a contextual tool column accompanies the score at regular width and becomes a dismissible panel at compact width, preserving page, selection, and undo history. Touch editing and keyboard commands reach the same operations.

Deliver a wide/narrow task flow and input mapping or corresponding implementation. Fail if shrinking loses a selected object, a pointer-only control blocks touch, or imported content silently replaces work. Use supplied evidence for findings; physical reach, Pencil response, and inter-app drag/drop remain unverified until exercised on supported devices.

Continue with [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md) for resizing, [Apple Pencil and Scribble](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-apple-pencil-and-scribble/SKILL.md) for drawing/writing, or [Pointing devices](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-pointing-devices/SKILL.md) for precision input.

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). For text reflow/type choices use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md); for a motion accommodation use [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md). If spatial comfort dominates the task, use [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md). Keep the task's accessibility acceptance checks when handing off.

# Make movement correspond to a meaningful value

Read [the slider guide](../../references/sliders.md). The workflow is application advice; apply only documented platform capabilities.

Inspect value meaning/units, minimum/maximum, step or continuous scale, precision needs, platform/input, and create/review/adapt mode. Determine whether the interval is bounded or wraps/repeats. Record the actual mapping and result feedback; track position alone does not prove a linear scale.

Use a slider for understandable bounded adjustment, with leading-to-trailing increase horizontally and bottom-to-top vertically. Pair wide ranges with exact numeric entry and useful increments when needed. On Mac choose linear for fixed intervals and circular for repeating/continuing values, explaining nonlinear mappings with intermediate labels. Provide live results where feasible and exact value exposure. Use the appropriate volume view for iOS/iPadOS audio output rather than rebuilding it as an arbitrary slider. Prefer horizontal adjustment on visionOS; define increments for the onscreen buttons beside the watch slider. Sliders are unsupported on tvOS in this guide.

Implement the mapping/feedback or supply range, scale, value, endpoint, and precision specifications; reviews must identify a concrete mapping or reachability defect. Avoid customization that hides the quantity or standard interaction.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a Mac opacity control uses a circular dial, has no value display, and makes 1% changes nearly impossible across a wide range. Decision: opacity is a fixed bounded interval and exact adjustment matters. After: use a linear 0–100% slider with live preview and a synchronized numeric field.

Deliver the artifact and mapping/precision contract. Verify endpoints, intermediate values, keyboard/assistive increments, numeric-field synchronization, and cancellation/undo if part of the product. Fail for inverted unexplained mapping, inaccessible required precision, or displayed/applied value disagreement. Report physical input/native value announcements separately.

Use [steppers](../apple-hig-steppers/SKILL.md) for small increments, [text-fields](../apple-hig-text-fields/SKILL.md) for precision, or [playing-audio](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-playing-audio/SKILL.md) for output-volume context.

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Designing for iPadOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. iPad supports portable entertainment, detailed work, and creative activity. Its large high-resolution display may be held, placed on a table, or used on a stand; typical viewing distance stays within about 3 feet. ## Best practices - Elevate useful content with the larger canvas. Reduce modal interruptions and full-screen transitions; keep controls reachable without obscuring the work. - Choose content density and sizing for both viewing distance and current input method. - Support combinations of touch, onscreen keyboard, attached keyboard, mouse or trackpad, Apple Pencil, and voice. Mixed-input workflows are normal. - Expect both quick actions and hours-long sessions. Support several visible apps, multitasking, and inter-app drag and drop rather than assuming exclusive use of the display. - Adapt continuously to orientation, multitasking sizes, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type. Preserve a coherent experience when the iPad app runs on macOS. - Consider widgets, multitasking support, and drag and drop as integrated parts of the experience. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here.

# Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Sliders Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sliders) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A slider uses a thumb on a track to adjust a bounded value. The filled leading portion indicates progress from the minimum, and endpoint glyphs can clarify the quantity. ## Best practices Customize track, thumb, tint, or endpoint imagery only when that improves meaning or integration. Horizontal minimum is at the leading side and maximum at the trailing side; vertical minimum is below maximum. Pair a wide-range slider with a numeric field for exact values and a stepper for convenient increments when helpful. ## Platform considerations Sliders are unsupported in tvOS. ### iOS, iPadOS For audio output volume, use a volume view, which combines a volume slider with an output-device control. ### macOS Linear sliders have a narrow lozenge thumb and optional ticks; circular sliders have a small circular thumb and optional evenly spaced dot ticks. Provide live result feedback when feasible. Use a linear control for a fixed bounded interval, such as 0–100% opacity, and a circular control for repeating or continuing values, such as 0–360° rotation or multiple full turns (4 turns = 1440°). A sentence-case introductory label normally ends in a colon. Ticks improve precision; label the endpoints or selected ticks instead of every tick unless all labels are needed. Nonlinear scales need enough intermediate labels to explain their mapping. A thumb tooltip can expose the exact current value. ### visionOS Prefer horizontal movement because side-to-side gestures are generally easier than vertical ones. ### watchOS A slider can show discrete steps or a continuous bar over a finite range. Buttons at its sides adjust by a defined amount. Replace the default plus/minus glyphs when custom glyphs better explain the function. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Steppers](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/steppers) [Pickers](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pickers) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 21, 2023.

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Consider spring loading through a dragged selection plus force-click on Magic Trackpad, preserving the drag afterward. #### Square buttons These small glyph-only controls affect a nearby view, for example adding/removing table rows. They can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls. Use them in the body rather than the frame, toolbar, or status bar. Prefer system symbols and omit introductory labels when proximity explains the function. #### Help buttons Use the familiar system question-mark control, at most one per window, opening context-specific help when possible and top-level help otherwise. In a dialog with dismissal controls, place it in the opposite lower corner, aligned vertically with those controls. Without dismissal controls, or in settings, use either lower corner. Keep it in the view body and omit explanatory introductory text. #### Image buttons Image buttons can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls inside a view. Toolbar imagery instead belongs to a toolbar item. Allow about 10 pixels between image and clickable button edges and generally omit a visible system border. Put any needed label beneath the image. ### visionOS Buttons normally have a visible background and audible feedback. Circle suits glyph-only content, rounded rectangle or capsule suits text, and capsule suits text plus glyph. Standard states supply feedback; custom hover effects are not supported. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. Use a discernible shape/fill except inside a larger clearly bounded toolbar, menu, alert, or ornament. On window glass, thin material suits the button; floating in space, use glass. Reserve white fill with black content for the system's toggled state. Prefer round/capsule forms for steady gaze, and a capsule for a standalone button. Keep centers at least 60 pt apart; add 4 pt padding around buttons 60 pt or larger to prevent hover overlap. Avoid rows/stacks of mini/small buttons. Prefer rounded rectangles for vertical text stacks and capsules for horizontal rows. Standard sounds matter because visionOS provides no haptics. ### watchOS Inline buttons are capsules with a contrasting material. Put corner actions in a toolbar so the system relocates title/time and gives controls Liquid Glass. Full-width buttons suit primary actions. Side-by-side buttons should share height and use short labels or glyphs; vertical one- and two-line buttons should also maintain common heights. Toolbar actions can navigate related areas or operate on current content. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Toggles](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toggles) [Segmented controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/segmented-controls) [Location button](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Location-button) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 16, 2025, June 9, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.

The specification will track playback intent separately from readiness and keep transcript position independent of video time, including during scrubbing and PiP transitions.

# iPad lecture reader: revised playback interaction specification

This replaces the behavior described in "'`interface.md`. It specifies interactions, not an SDK implementation. The only product evidence is that short brief; duration, media format, implementation, caption availability, and PiP capability are unknown. Assume an on-demand lecture with a seekable timeline when its duration is known.

## Decisions and source basis

1. Open the lecture silently in Ready, at its saved playback time, with Play visible. Do not autoplay on entry, return, resize, or lecture completion. This is a product decision to fix unexpected loud playback, informed by [Accessibility — Cognitive](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Cognitive). Deliberately played lecture audio is essential media: use playback-like audio behavior, respect the selected output and system volume, and never raise global volume. Silent mode need not suppress deliberately initiated lecture audio. See [Playing audio — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio#Best-practices).
2. Prefer a system player when the chosen environment supplies one; otherwise reproduce familiar transport behavior through a capability adapter. No Apple SDK is assumed. Keep captions, controls, and useful metadata from obscuring one another; preserve original aspect ratio without baked-in bars. For lecture slides, choose aspect-fit to preserve all slide text (a product choice). The local video source describes overlapping defaults at exactly 2:1; do not invent an exclusive rule there. See [Playing video — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-video#Best-practices).
3. Separate media time from transcript reading position. Seeking never silently scrolls the transcript. Preserve both across exits, interruptions, and resizing. This applies [Multitasking — Best practices and iPadOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/multitasking#iPadOS) to the reader'"'s task.
4. Represent loading, buffering, pause, interruption, and failure distinctly. Keep available transcript content usable while media waits. Use text plus an indeterminate activity indication when the wait duration is unknown; never invent a percentage or ETA. See [Loading — Showing progress](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/loading#Showing-progress).
5. Captions convey synchronized audible information; a transcript remains a separate reading resource, not a substitute for captions. Preserve caption preferences, expose unavailable tracks honestly, and support text enlargement. See [Accessibility — Hearing and Vision](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Hearing).

## State and persistence contract

Use orthogonal state so a single “paused” flag cannot hide a stall:

"'```text
intent = stopped | play
transport = ready | loading | playing | paused | buffering |
            seeking | interrupted | ended | error
presentation = inline | pipStarting | pip | pipReturning
confirmedTime, duration?, pendingSeek?, requestGeneration
reader = {segmentId, offsetWithinSegment, selection, follow: off|on}
preferences = {captionTrack, captionStyle, playbackRate}
interruption = {reason, wasPlaying, resumePermitted}
```

Save lecture ID, confirmed media time, reader anchor/selection, and preferences on pause, committed seek, exit, and lifecycle loss; checkpoint confirmed time during playback. Never persist an unconfirmed seek as the resume time. On reopening, restore the reader anchor independently and enter Ready, even if the last session was playing. If an anchor'"'s segment is missing, restore the nearest preceding available segment and explain the fallback. If duration changed, clamp resume time to the new duration and show the adjusted time. A completed lecture opens Ended with Replay, without starting another lecture.

Only actual media-clock advancement establishes Playing. "'`intent=play` alone does not. Status labels are persistent while applicable and do not depend on color or animation. Last frame/poster stays visible during waits; never present frozen media as successful playback.

| Event / current condition | Result and visible interaction |
|---|---|
| Open lecture | Ready, “Play” (or “Resume” with saved time); transcript immediately usable if available. Fetch metadata/initial media independently; do not download the entire lecture before enabling playback. |
| Play / Ready or Paused | Set intent=play. If data is ready, request playback; otherwise Loading with “Loading video…” and a Pause action that cancels play intent. |
| Clock advances / intent=play | Playing; Pause is the main transport action. |
| Data starvation / intent=play | Buffering; show “Buffering…” and activity feedback in the media status area, with Pause available. Preserve confirmed time and reader anchor. |
| Pause / Playing, Loading, Buffering | Set intent=stopped; halt output and enter Paused. Show “Paused” and Play. Later readiness cannot restart it. |
| Data ready / Buffering or Loading | Resume only if intent is still play and no interruption/error blocks it; otherwise remain Paused. |
| Begin scrub | Capture confirmed time, intent, and reader anchor; suspend output; enter Seeking. Preview candidate time without committing reader movement. |
| Commit scrub | Clamp target to [0,duration]; issue one seek with a new generation. Show “Seeking to mm:ss…” until confirmed. On confirmation update confirmedTime; restore captured intent unless the person paused or an interruption intervened. Wait for data if needed. |
| Cancel scrub / Escape or visible Cancel Seek | Restore prior confirmed time and captured intent, subject to later pause/interruption; reader stays at its original anchor. |
| Seek failure | Error with “Couldn’t seek. Retry” and last confirmed time retained. Intent becomes stopped. Retry repeats the target, then returns paused; Play remains a separate choice. |
| Media/network failure | Error, “Video unavailable” with contextual reason when known, Retry, and preserved transcript. Clear play intent. Retry enters Loading, suppresses duplicate requests, and returns Ready/Paused on success. Never leave a permanent spinner after a reported failure. |
| No readiness or progress for 15 seconds | Offer “Still waiting for video” with Retry and Stop Waiting. This is a proposed product timeout, not an Apple requirement. Stop Waiting preserves context and pauses; no false offline claim. |
| Media reaches end | Ended, intent=stopped; Replay seeks to zero and plays only on activation. Keep transcript anchor. |
| Leave reader / Back | Pause unless confirmed PiP owns playback. Save state and return to the containing lecture/course context; rapid exit during loading must work. |

On any new lecture, retry, or seek, invalidate obsolete asynchronous completions. Apply callbacks only to their lecture ID and generation. A late callback must never undo Pause, select an old lecture, move the reader, or restart sound. When a temporary interruption arrives during seeking, its pause policy overrides the captured scrub intent.

## Reader, captions, and controls

The default transcript mode is independent reading (`follow=off`). Playback may mark the current spoken segment without scrolling or moving focus. “Follow Playback” explicitly scrolls to the current segment and enables following; manual transcript scrolling switches it off. “Return to Reading Position” restores the anchor saved when following began and turns following off. A timestamp action seeks media to that segment; it does not change the transcript viewport. PiP time updates obey the same rule.

In a wide window, show video and transcript together. In a narrow window, stack them in one reader flow, keeping a persistent compact transport area. Resizing or orientation changes retain time, pending state, reader anchor, selection, and caption preferences. Choose arrangement from available space rather than inferring the user'"'s multitasking configuration. See [Designing for iPadOS — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados#Best-practices).

Reserve a caption region clear of the control and status regions. Controls and buffering/error messages must never cover caption glyphs, including at 200% text size and narrow widths. Reflow the player/controls or move controls below the video when space is insufficient; do not shrink captions to fit. Fit the video without cropping slide edges. Captions track confirmed presentation time; do not advance them with a scrub preview. If a requested track is absent, show “Captions unavailable” and retain the saved preference for future lectures. Preserve system caption preferences where the environment exposes them; an adapter must report its actual capabilities.

| Control | Contract |
|---|---|
| Play / Pause / Replay | One prominent transport button; its name states the action, while a separate status states reality. During delayed initial Play, retain its context and show activity with “Loading”; Pause remains operable. |
| Timeline | Labeled “Playback position”, linear 0–duration, increasing from leading to trailing edge; expose current and preview mm:ss (hh:mm:ss when needed). Disable seeking with “Seeking unavailable” until bounds/capability are known. |
| Back 10 Seconds / Forward 10 Seconds | Visible alternatives to precision dragging; clamp to bounds. Keyboard/assistive timeline increments are 1 second. These intervals are product choices. |
| Follow Playback / Return to Reading Position | Explicit reading actions as specified above; no hidden gesture required. |
| Retry / Stop Waiting | Retry only the failed media operation; activity feedback while pending. Stop Waiting clears intent and pending work without resetting reading context. |
| Picture in Picture | Offer only when capability is reported. Starting is pending until confirmed; failure returns inline with an explanation and the same time/intent. |

Use at least 44 × 44 pt nonoverlapping activation regions for these iPad controls, with clear separation, press feedback, and visible keyboard focus. Icon controls require action names. This adopts the default iPad control size rather than the smaller accessibility minimum; see [Buttons — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons#Best-practices) and [Accessibility — Mobility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility#Mobility). Timeline quantity and endpoint behavior follow [Sliders — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sliders#Best-practices).

Touch and pointer activate the same visible actions; hover is never required. With playback context active and focus outside editable text, Space toggles playback; do not intercept Space for transcript text editing or system accessibility commands. All actions must be reachable by keyboard and assistive input. Expose status text, action names, enabled/pending states, and timeline role/range/value; announce state changes without announcing every clock tick. Keep controls available while focused rather than timing them out.
